display: I'm a buyer for the shops of four London museums. I look for objects with a named maker, and I have little patience for mass-made 'heritage'.

signals.text: I need makers, not a catalogue: people whose work I can name, not agencies who resell it.
I'm trying to cut generic 'heritage' stock in our shops from about forty percent to under twenty this buying round.
I'm planning a themed range of Asian handwork for next year, tied to a spring exhibition. It is small in volume but strict on provenance.
I can't find anyone who offers maker-signed embroidery in batches of 300 or more. Single makers can't reach that number, and the agencies that can won't show me who made the thing.
Merchandising wants volumes, lead times and price points by 15 October, and I don't have the batch and timeline numbers to give them yet.
I'm looking for English-language maker-story cards and packaging that passes a plastic-free rule, ideally from the maker's side or arranged with them.
I'm reading about Karen weaving and Hmong stitch work. It's early, and I'm still working out what is feasible for a retail cycle.
I'd like to meet textile and embroidery workshops that answer email reliably and can commit to a retail calendar. Lovely studios that reply slowly don't fit a retail cycle.
I'm worried the themed range will end up filled with the generic stock I'm trying to get rid of, simply because I can't find enough volume.
Merchandising is pushing for volume, and I'm caught between their numbers and my provenance rule.
I'm restoring a 1962 narrowboat at weekends and could use advice on old paint, possibly lead, and on boat engines and pumps.
I'm learning Japanese on my commute, slowly and badly, and enjoying it anyway.

offers.text: I buy across four London museum shops, with two seasonal ranges a year. I can put a maker in front of a real buyer and a real shelf.
I trained in textile conservation and can tell hand embroidery from machine work at arm's length, so I can tell you honestly what your work looks like to a buyer.
I keep a notebook of about two hundred makers worldwide, many reached through personal introductions, and I can introduce makers to each other when it fits.
I know retail compliance in practice: plastic-free packaging rules, labelling and product-safety paperwork. I can explain what a supplier needs to get through it.
I have working relationships with three small London printers who produce maker-story cards.
I can explain what a museum-shop range needs from a maker: named provenance, batch size, lead time, packaging and story card.
I can give honest feedback on whether a product reads as 'heritage-style' stock or as an object with a named maker.

catchers.hypo: I run an embroidery cooperative of about thirty women in northern Thailand. Every piece is signed or traceable to the maker, and we can do 300 or more per batch with a few months' notice. Would a museum shop be interested?
catchers.can: I'd bring it to my planning for the 'Hands of Asia' range and check whether it meets the batch size, packaging and story-card needs. If it does, I'd take it to a supplier meeting and to merchandising.
catchers.confirm: Can the maker of each piece be named, and can you deliver at least 300 units in a single batch?

catchers.hypo: I work with several craft groups across Southeast Asia and can organise batches, packaging and English documentation, while keeping each maker visible and credited. Is that of interest?
catchers.can: I'd consider you as a way to reach volume without losing provenance, and test it with a small first order.
catchers.confirm: Can you show me, for a given batch, which individual maker produced which piece?

catchers.hypo: I make plastic-free packaging for handmade goods and have sold to small brands. Do museum shops need this?
catchers.can: I can check whether your packaging meets our group's plastic-free rules and put you forward for the packaging side of the range.
catchers.confirm: Does your packaging contain no plastic at all, including films, tapes and fillers?

catchers.hypo: I translate and design maker-story cards for craft producers abroad, with the maker's voice kept in English. Can you use that?
catchers.can: I could connect you with the story-card needs of the range, and with the London printers I already work with.
catchers.confirm: Can you produce English cards that quote or describe the individual maker, not just the region or the craft tradition?

catchers.hypo: I'm a craftsperson who has been told my work is too small-scale for shops. Could I ever sell through a museum?
catchers.can: I can tell you honestly what a museum shop looks for, what batch sizes and lead times it needs, and whether your work could fit now or later. If not, I may know another maker or buyer who is a better match.
catchers.confirm: Is your work made by you or a named small team, in a way you could describe and show?

catchers.hypo: I'm a buyer at a small independent shop, tired of the same 'artisan' stock at every trade fair. How do you tell what's real?
catchers.can: I can share how I check for hand work and a named maker, and compare notes on which fairs and supplier routes are worth the time.
catchers.confirm: Do you buy for a shop where provenance matters more to you than price per unit?

catchers.hypo: I'm restoring an old wooden boat and found old paint with something yellow underneath. Has anyone dealt with this?
catchers.can: I'm in the same position myself, so I can swap notes. My marina neighbour Colin, a retired boat-builder, may be able to advise or point you to someone.
catchers.confirm: Is the boat an older timber or steel narrowboat, and do you want to compare notes on testing old paint for lead?

catchers.hypo: I tutor GCSE maths for teenagers who are anxious and dislike reassurance. I don't do pep talks, only clear practice and a calm pace.
catchers.can: I could pass this on to someone close to me who is facing exactly that, and let them decide.
catchers.confirm: Do you teach in a way that avoids reassurance and focuses on practical steps, for a student who is shaky in maths?

forbids.text: I won't buy goods whose maker can't be named.
I won't stock packaging that fails the shop group's plastic-free rules.
I can't commit a range to merchandising without batch sizes and lead times.
I don't buy 'heritage-style' goods or digitally printed items presented as hand-made.
I won't share supplier prices or margin targets with anyone outside the buying team.

projects.name: Hands of Asia
projects.text: A themed range for next year tied to a spring exhibition. Every object carries a named maker. Volume is thin but provenance is strict.
roles_needed: Embroidery or textile maker group able to do 300+ units per batch with named makers
Coordinator who keeps individual makers visible at volume
English maker-story card writer or translator
Export and shipping handler for small craft batches

policy.t1: When there's a real lead, I'll share what a themed museum-shop range requires: named maker, batch size, packaging, story cards and rough timelines.
policy.t2: Once the match looks strong and I know who you are, I'll share more about my situation: pressure from merchandising, family, and the narrowboat.
policy.never: Supplier prices and margin targets, and any private details about my family.
